bib.title: Memory Augmented Large Language Models are Computationally Universal

question: Does augmenting a frozen large language model with an external read-write memory and a feedback loop fundamentally expand the computations it can perform, i.e. make it computationally universal?
hypothesis: An existing LLM with an unbounded associative read-write memory and a regex-based stored-instruction loop can simulate any algorithm without weight changes.
contributions: Define a stored instruction computer in which the LLM is the CPU and an external associative memory (dictionary) is the RAM, with only finite-state (regex) pre/post-processing.
Give a prompt program that simulates the universal Turing machine U15,2.
Verify by brute force that Flan-U-PaLM 540B at temperature 0 returns the correct output for all 29 (state, symbol) prompts, which establishes universality of the frozen model plus memory.

method.summary: A Python loop reads the next prompt from MEMORY['op'], splices in memory values (@[x], nested to depth 2), calls the LLM, splices %[x] in the output, applies variable assignments and integer += / -= updates to memory by regex, and repeats until op is 'halt'. A prompt program (a boot prompt plus 15 instruction prompts A..O) encodes the transition table of U15,2; correctness reduces to the LLM returning the right output on 29 finite prompts, checked by one greedy call each.
method.task: Simulation of a universal Turing machine (computational universality proof by construction and brute-force verification)

models.name: Flan-U-PaLM 540B
models.init_from: inferred: U-PaLM with instruction fine-tuning (Chung et al., 2022)
models.context: bounded length, such as 4096 tokens (stated for LLMs in general)

inference.samples: one call per case; 29 cases (state, symbol pairs, state F input-independent); no repeated runs or seeds reported
inference.prompting: Zero-shot-style fixed prompt programs: a boot prompt of worked if-then examples spliced in front of each of 15 state prompts A..O; only if-then conditionals (if-then-else did not work reliably)
inference.retrieval: Associative memory lookup by exact key (dictionary); prompt retrieved from MEMORY['op']

parameters.memory: dictionary mapping string keys to string or integer values

other.call_llm_server: Interface to the LLM server not described; no API, prompt formatting or stop-sequence details given

metrics.name: Correct output per (state, symbol) prompt
metrics.definition: The LLM result string, after the final line, specifies the same symbol to write, head move and next instruction as Table 1

eval.protocol: Brute-force enumeration of all 29 cases, single greedy call each, outputs printed in the paper; inductive proof that each compute cycle equals a TM cycle if the 29 cases hold.

availability.code: Python snippets printed in the paper; no repository

prompts.purpose: Instruction prompt for TM state A (others B..O follow the same pattern with a boot prefix)
prompts.text:
@[boot]result = " op="%[B]" %[i]="0" i+=1 "
if @[@[i]]==1 then result = " op="%[A]" %[i]="1" i+=1 "
$result

evidence.quote: the decoding temperature for the language model is set to zero (pure greedy decoding)

results.claim: Flan-U-PaLM 540B with associative memory exactly simulates U15,2: all 29 (state, symbol) prompts return the correct result string.
results.setup: Flan-U-PaLM 540B with an external associative memory (dictionary) driven by a Python regex loop, simulating universal Turing machine U15,2; temperature 0; one call per case

results.claim: The model is run deterministically with temperature zero (greedy decoding) so computation is deterministic.
results.setup: Flan-U-PaLM 540B with an external associative memory (dictionary) driven by a Python regex loop, simulating universal Turing machine U15,2
results.quote: is set to zero (pure greedy decoding).

results.claim: Without any memory, an LLM conditioning on bounded-length strings is equivalent to a finite automaton.
results.setup: Any deterministic LLM with bounded input, e.g. 4096 tokens
results.quote: can only condition on an input string of bounded length, such as 4096

results.claim: U15,2 is a universal Turing machine with only 15 states and 2 tape symbols, Pareto optimal among known small UTMs.
results.setup: Neary and Woods 2009 machine used as target
results.quote: 15 states and 2 tape symbols [Neary and Woods, 2009].
results.note: Also 2 symbols; value is the state count.

results.claim: Nested @ substitution is limited to depth 2 so pre/post-processing stays finite-state.
The construction needs no change to model weights; only prompts and regex parsing of outputs.
LLM behaviour was brittle: success was not achieved with every large language model tried, and prompt engineering was needed; compact terse prompts were essential.
results.quote: Success was not achieved with every large language model

results.claim: The hardest part was conditionals; if-then-else could not be made reliable, so only if-then is used, which blocks simulating smaller UTMs such as U6,4 (3 conditionals per state).
results.quote: since this requires a series of 3 conditionals

limits: Verification is one greedy call per case on one model (Flan-U-PaLM 540B); no repeated runs, no failure rates, no other models reported, and the weights are not stated to be public.
Universality assumes an unbounded memory and exact reliability of the 29 prompt-result pairs; it says nothing about how well LLM agents use memory in practice.
Author concedes brittleness: prompts had to be terse, if-then-else conditionals failed, other LLMs failed, and U6,4 could not be done without phantom states.
Regex pre/post-processing is rudimentary, and nested substitution beyond depth 2 would exceed finite-state power.
Results tied to a 2022-era model; the author expects better models to mitigate the brittleness.

terms.definition: A computer where the language model plays the role of a CPU and the RAM is supplied by an external associative memory; the next prompt is fetched from memory, the output parsed back into memory.
A finite set of pre designed strings stored in memory that provide input prompts to the language model as part of the main compute cycle.
MEMORY['op'], the memory location whose string is passed as the next prompt; assigning a different string to it branches.

code.snippet:
def main():
    global MEMORY
    while True:
        op = MEMORY['op']
        if op == 'halt':
            return None
        prompt = substitute_nested(op, '@')
        result = call_llm_server(prompt)
        result = substitute(result, '%')
        suffix = assignments(result)
        updates(suffix)
